fact: CSU Extension's landscape design notes call the front yard the public area of a landscape, openly viewed by others, say homeowners' associations and cities often regulate what can be done there, and tell designers to ask whether codes or covenants apply and whether the plan should match the neighborhood's style.
quote: Do any municipal codes or subdivision covenants apply? … Should the planned landscaping match the neighborhood landscape style? … The public area, typically the front yard is openly viewed by others. Homeowners’ associations and cities often regulate what can and cannot be done in the public area of landscapes.
source_label: CSU Extension, Water-Wise Landscape Design: Steps (Garden Notes; published October 2014, reviewed July 2025)
notes: Read with curl 2026-09-25 (HTTP 200). Authors John Murgel, David Whiting, Jeffry de Jong; reviewed by Chris Hilgert. Step 1 (site analysis, 'The Extended Landscape') and Step 3 (public, private and utility areas).

fact: CSU Extension says water-wise landscaping is not necessarily against turf but matches the design to how the site is actually used, a change from designs where a little-used but high-input lawn is the main feature.
quote: Water-wise landscaping is not necessarily anti-turf, but rather matches the landscape design to the actual use of the site. This is a change from the typical landscape design where a little-used but high input lawn is the predominant feature.
source_label: CSU Extension, Water-Wise Landscape Design: Steps (Garden Notes; published October 2014, reviewed July 2025)
notes: The page means living turf; the guide uses it for the design principle (fit the surface to the use), not as a statement about artificial turf.

fact: CSU Extension advises refining a landscape in one design style, rectilinear, curvilinear or angular, and using features on the home as size references to keep garden elements in scale.
quote: Using your bubble drawing, begin to define spaces, using a single design style in order to maintain garden coherence. For example: Rectilinear style has straight lines and right angles in square and rectangular shapes. Curvilinear style avoids straight lines and right angles using bold sweeping curves instead. Angular style uses straight lines but with a variety of angles and directions. The property line and the home style do not dictate the landscape style but can help inform it. Use features on the home as size references to keep garden elements in scale.
source_label: CSU Extension, Water-Wise Landscape Design: Steps (Garden Notes; published October 2014, reviewed July 2025), Step 3b

fact: CSU Extension advises against designing small irrigated areas less than about eight feet wide or irregularly shaped, and says any that can't be avoided should be designed for drip irrigation or hand-watering.
quote: In design, avoid creating small (less than about eight feet wide), irregularly shaped areas that will require irrigation. If such areas are unavoidable, design them for drip irrigation or hand-watering.
source_label: CSU Extension, Water-Wise Landscape Design: Steps (Garden Notes; published October 2014, reviewed July 2025), Step 3c

fact: The City of Longmont makes the resident keep a clear line of access to the water meter, remove landscaping or materials blocking an outdoor meter, sod and yard edging included, and keep the meter at finished ground level, or the City does the work and bills the cost plus a 25 percent surcharge.
quote: It is the responsibility of the resident occupying the property to maintain a clear line of access to the water meter at all times. … If the resident doesn’t remove the obstruction, the City shall perform the work subject to reimbursement of cost plus a twenty-five percent surcharge. Outdoors – the resident must remove any landscaping or materials blocking the water meter. This can include but isn’t limited to bushes, flowers, trees, fences, sod, yard edging, concrete or cement blocks. The resident must also ensure the water meter is at finished ground level.
source_label: City of Longmont, Water Meter Maintenance Program
notes: Read with curl 2026-09-25 (HTTP 200). Longmont's own customers only; other providers were not checked, so the guide tells readers to ask their water provider.

fact: Greeley planning staff summarize the current front-yard standard for houses as at most 50% hardscape with the rest in planting areas, 50% live planting coverage in those areas, no bare earth, one tree if space allows and no artificial turf, and say streetscape planters also need 50% plants, groundcover and trees every 25 to 35 feet.
quote: Draft Landscape Code EXISTING • Front yards of houses • Maximum 50% hardscape, remainder must be planting areas • 50% live planting coverage in planting areas • No bare earth, all areas need covered with live plantings, mulch, rock, or hardscape • Artificial turf prohibited • One tree required if space allows • Streetscape planters also need 50% plants, groundcover, and trees every 25-35 feet
source_label: Greeley Planning Commission agenda packet, July 14, 2026, staff slide "Draft Landscape Code" (existing front-yard standards for houses)
notes: Read from the packet PDF (pdftotext) 2026-09-25, the same file as greeley-front-yard-ban-city-summary. A staff summary slide, not code text; the same slide lists the proposed change ('Artificial turf with a permit'; 'Clarify that 50% live plantings must be perennial'). Re-check with the Greeley initiative records.

fact: Harvest's Declaration in Berthoud requires foundation plantings along street frontages at 10 plants per 40 linear feet of foundation, a mix of deciduous and evergreen shrubs with perennials and ornamental grasses.
quote: Foundation plantings adjacent to the current and future street frontages are required to be planted with a mixture of deciduous and evergreen shrubs with accents of perennials and ornamental grasses at a rate of 10 plants per 40 linear feet of foundation.
source_label: Declaration of Covenants, Conditions, and Restrictions for Harvest (recorded July 1, 2021, Larimer County Reception No. 20210063769), Sec. 2.19, Landscaping (private lot landscaping)
notes: Scanned PDF (the link redirects to squarespace static storage); page 10 rendered with pdftoppm and read as an image 2026-09-25. Side yards away from the street: 5 plants per 40 linear feet; rear yards: 8 per 40.
